issues.legal_issue: A land acquisition notification need not state whether the land is arable or waste land.
material_facts: The acquisition notification stated that the land was needed for a public purpose but did not specify whether it was arable or waste land.
The High Court quashed the notification in part because it did not declare the nature of the land.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to require the notification to specify the nature of the land.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 requires publication to notify interested persons that land is needed or likely to be needed for a public purpose, authorise entry for measurement and related work, and notify owners that later encumbrances will not bind the State. It does not require a statement whether the land is arable or waste land.

predicates.land_acquisition_notification: The government published a notification announcing that land was needed or likely to be needed for a public purpose.

issues.definition: When a government publishes a land acquisition notification, it need not describe the land's type.

issues.legal_issue: Land capable of cultivation may be treated as arable for an urgent acquisition even when it is situated in an urban area and includes some buildings.
material_facts: The acquired tract included six acres belonging to the respondents and formed part of a larger area.
The respondents' land consisted of open land as well as buildings and servant quarters, but the buildings were not acquired for the public purpose and only the servant quarters were acquired.
The land was capable of raising crops, although it was situated in an urban area.
The High Court held that the land was not arable or waste land and that dispensing with the inquiry was unlawful.
issues.conclusion: The land was arable because it was capable of cultivation, and the exercise of the power to dispense with the inquiry was not bad in law; the High Court's contrary view was erroneous.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 17(4) and 5-A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 govern dispensing with the inquiry. Whether land is arable or waste is a mixed question of fact and law that depends on the circumstances; a pragmatic assessment is required, and land capable of raising crops may be arable even in an urban area. The Court relied on Ishwarlal Girdharilal Joshi v. State of Gujarat, (1968) 2 SCR 267, and Raja Anand Brahma Shah v. State of Uttar Pradesh, AIR 1967 SC 1801.

predicates.urgent_land_acquisition_case: The government acquired land for a public purpose using an urgent procedure that dispensed with the usual inquiry.
predicates.land_capable_of_cultivation: The acquired land was capable of being cultivated, whether or not it was situated in an urban area.

issues.definition: In an urgent land acquisition case, if the land is capable of cultivation, dispensing with the inquiry is valid.

issues.legal_issue: A defect in local publication does not require a court to quash a completed acquisition where possession has been taken and the acquisition and compensation proceedings have become final.
material_facts: The substance of the acquisition notification was not published in the locality; the Court proceeded on that premise and treated local publication as mandatory.
Possession had been taken, the land had vested in the State, and the acquisition proceedings had become final.
The respondents sought a compensation reference, accepted the court's enhanced compensation award, and the subsequent appellate proceedings had become final.
The respondents later challenged the acquisition by writ petition, and the High Court quashed the notification and declaration.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have quashed the notification and declaration; the appeal was allowed and the writ petition was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4(1) and 6 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 concern the notification and declaration; Sections 16 and 17 provide for vesting following possession, and Section 48(1) permits withdrawal before possession is taken. Under Article 226, relief is discretionary: even where an action is void or a mandatory requirement was not met, a court may refuse to quash it because of delay, acquiescence, waiver, finality, or other relevant circumstances. The Court relied on Sanjeevanagar Medical & Health Employees' Co-operative Society v. Mohd. Abdul Wahab, (1996) 3 SCC 600; Satendra Prasad Jain v. State of U.P., (1993) 4 SCC 369; Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay v. Industrial Development & Investment Co. (P) Ltd. (decided September 6, 1996); M.P. Housing Board v. Mohd. Shafi, (1992) 2 SCC 168; Nutakki Sesharatanam v. Sub-Collector, L.A., Vijayawada, (1992) 1 SCC 114, whose ratio the Court rejected; and H.W.R. Wade, Administrative Law, 7th ed., pp. 342–43. The Court distinguished Ujjain Vikas Pradhikaran v. Raj Kumar Johri, (1992) 1 SCC 328, because the compensation award there had not yet been made.

rule.if: acquisition_writ_challenge and local_publication_omitted and possession_taken and acquisition_proceedings_final and compensation_proceedings_final

predicates.acquisition_writ_challenge: An interested person challenged a land acquisition by seeking discretionary writ relief.
predicates.local_publication_omitted: The acquiring authority did not publish the substance of the acquisition notice in the locality.
predicates.possession_taken: The acquiring authority took possession of the land and the land vested in the State.
predicates.acquisition_proceedings_final: The steps in the acquisition had become final by the time the court considered the challenge.
predicates.compensation_proceedings_final: The compensation determination and any related appellate proceedings had become final.

issues.definition: When a person seeks writ relief against an acquisition despite omitted local publication, the court should decline to quash it if possession has been taken and both the acquisition and compensation proceedings are final.
